name: cutaneous b cell lymphoma
aliases: primary cutaneous marginal zone / follicle centre / leg-type lymphoma

reference.source: WHO-EORTC classification of cutaneous lymphomas / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: Primary cutaneous B-cell lymphomas are non-Hodgkin lymphomas that arise in and are confined to the skin at presentation, so accurate staging to exclude systemic lymphoma with secondary cutaneous spread is essential before labelling disease as primary cutaneous

The WHO-EORTC scheme recognises three principal entities: primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma and primary cutaneous follicle centre lymphoma, both indolent, and primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type, which is aggressive

Indolent forms present as solitary or clustered erythematous to violaceous papules, plaques or nodules, favouring the trunk and scalp in follicle centre lymphoma and the trunk and arms in marginal zone lymphoma

Leg-type diffuse large B-cell lymphoma typically affects elderly women as rapidly growing red-blue tumours on one or both lower legs and carries a markedly worse outlook, though morphologically identical tumours can arise elsewhere

Immunophenotype separates the subtypes: follicle centre lymphoma is BCL6 positive with variable CD10 and usually lacks strong BCL2, marginal zone lymphoma shows monotypic light-chain restriction with plasmacytic differentiation, and leg type expresses strong BCL2, MUM1/IRF4 and FOXP1
Primary cutaneous marginal zone lymphoma has been linked to Borrelia burgdorferi infection in some endemic regions, and antibiotic therapy has occasionally induced regression
Indolent forms are treated with skin-directed measures such as excision, radiotherapy or intralesional therapy, whereas leg type requires systemic anthracycline-based chemoimmunotherapy
reference.pathophysiology: Cutaneous B-cell lymphomas result from clonal proliferation of B lymphocytes at differing stages of maturation that home to and expand within the skin. Marginal zone lymphoma derives from post-germinal-centre marginal zone / memory B cells and may be driven by chronic antigenic stimulation, including Borrelia in endemic areas. Follicle centre lymphoma arises from germinal-centre B cells but, unlike its nodal follicular counterpart, usually lacks the t(14;18) BCL2 rearrangement. Leg-type diffuse large B-cell lymphoma originates from activated non-germinal-centre B cells, characteristically over-expressing BCL2 and MUM1/IRF4 and frequently harbouring MYD88 mutation and other lesions that drive constitutive NF-kB signalling, underlying its aggressive behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous T-cell lymphoma, including mycosis fungoides and CD30-positive lymphoproliferative disorders
Systemic nodal B-cell lymphoma with secondary cutaneous involvement
Leukaemia cutis or B-lymphoblastic lymphoma involving skin
Cutaneous sarcoidosis or other granulomatous infiltrates
Persistent arthropod-bite reaction or nodular scabies
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy with histology and a broad immunohistochemical panel (CD20, CD79a, BCL2, BCL6, CD10, MUM1/IRF4, FOXP1, kappa and lambda light chains)
B-cell clonality assessment by immunoglobulin heavy-chain gene rearrangement studies
Staging cross-sectional imaging or PET-CT to exclude nodal or visceral lymphoma
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine, particularly for leg type or when systemic disease is suspected
Full blood count, lactate dehydrogenase and serum protein electrophoresis
Borrelia burgdorferi serology or tissue PCR in marginal zone lymphoma from endemic regions
MYD88 mutation analysis in suspected leg-type diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging red-blue tumour on the lower leg of an elderly patient, suggesting aggressive leg-type disease
Ulceration, systemic B symptoms or a rising lactate dehydrogenase
Lymphadenopathy or organomegaly indicating possible systemic dissemination
Extracutaneous involvement detected on staging investigations
reference.prognosis: Primary cutaneous marginal zone and follicle centre lymphomas are indolent with excellent long-term survival despite frequent cutaneous relapses, whereas primary cutaneous diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, leg type, has a substantially poorer prognosis, worsened by multiple lesions and leg location.
pitfalls: Misclassifying a systemic lymphoma with skin involvement as primary cutaneous by omitting adequate staging
Confusing reactive cutaneous lymphoid hyperplasia with a low-grade B-cell lymphoma
Over-treating indolent disease with aggressive systemic chemotherapy
Assuming BCL2 positivity necessarily indicates nodal follicular lymphoma
Missing leg-type diffuse large B-cell lymphoma when the tumours arise outside the lower legs
management: Accurate staging to exclude systemic lymphoma before treating disease as primary cutaneous

Local radiotherapy or surgical excision for solitary or clustered indolent marginal zone or follicle centre lesions, with intralesional or topical corticosteroids and active observation as alternatives
Antibiotic therapy directed at Borrelia in marginal zone lymphoma from endemic regions
Rituximab anti-CD20 therapy for multifocal or relapsing indolent disease
Anthracycline-based immunochemotherapy such as R-CHOP, with radiotherapy, for aggressive leg-type diffuse large B-cell lymphoma
Surveillance for cutaneous relapse and for systemic progression
Care through a dermatology and haemato-oncology multidisciplinary team
